**Long Distance**

My mother has called me every November 9th since 2003, from a payphone outside the Blue Jay, a diner that burned down in 1994. I know the diner's gone because I drove past the lot once, back in the year when I still needed proof of things. There's a weed-choked foundation and a sign for a self-storage company. There is no phone.

The first call came at 6:14 in the evening. Four rings—I counted them, because I count things—and then her voice, mid-sentence, picking up a conversation we'd apparently left dangling for days: "—so anyway, tell me about the apartment." Not hello. Never hello. My mother considered greetings a waste of breath.

She had maybe three minutes. I could hear coins moving through her hands, that clatter and drop, and I understood even then not to ask why. So I told her about the apartment, the radiator that knocked like a polite ghost. She laughed at "polite ghost" in exactly her way, a little honk at the top, and the line went dead between one laugh and the next. I sat on the floor holding the phone for a long time.

I tried calling back. The number, said the recording, has been disconnected. It said it gently, twice.

The second year I waited all day beside the phone. Four rings. "So did you ever fix that radiator?"

Over the years I've learned the rules the way you learn anything that matters: by breaking them. Rule one, answer by the fourth ring, or nothing until next November. I tested that once, the year I couldn't stand the wanting anymore, and paid for it with twelve months of silence, during which I learned that hope is a muscle and it atrophies. Rule two, never say how long it's been. The one time I slipped—"God, Mom, it's been twenty years"—she paused, confused, hurt, and then static rose up the line like water filling a sink, and I lost her early. Rule three: no questions about after. I asked once, softly, "Mom, where are you, are you okay," and got the dial tone, flat and final as a dropped lid.

Rule four took longest: ask small questions. The big ones starve her. Did she find the blue scarf she lost in 1987? Yes—in her coat pocket, of course. Had Mr. Alvarez next door fixed his gutter? He had not; he'd put up a plastic owl instead. She told me the owl worked, which we both understood to be a lie, and I loved her so much in that moment I had to press my palm flat on the table to keep from making a sound.

Once, on her second call, she mentioned snow. Later I went to the library and pulled the microfilm: November 9th, 1989, four inches, earliest storm in the county's records. I stopped needing proof after that. Needing proof is just another way of asking the universe to flatter you.

I keep a notebook now. Questions accumulate all year and get ranked. In the early days the list was desperate: *Are you happy. Do you know I'm sorry. Should I take the job in Denver.* Now the entries read more like weather: *Ask about the owl. Ask if she remembers the beach house, the sand in the eggs.* Ask her to hum *it*—the tuneless half-song she hummed while cooking. She'll say she doesn't remember humming anything. Then she'll hum.

Last year I noticed something I'd been avoiding. I'm fifty-four now. She was fifty-three when the Blue Jay burned. Somewhere between one November and the next I aged past her, and when she says *You sound tired, honey*, it comes down from somewhere above me—a hand resting on the head of a grown man kneeling in his own kitchen.

Here is what I know about the calls, or believe, which may amount to the same thing: it's not a message system. I used to hunt for meaning in every phrase—*does she know, can she see me, is this purgatory or a porch*. I gave that up. What I've settled on is simpler and much harder. It's just her, with a handful of change, doing the thing she always did, which was check on me. Three minutes of checking on me. Everything else is my side of the wire.

November 9th falls on a Sunday this year. I've cleaned the apartment the way you would if company were coming, which is ridiculous, and I've done it anyway. The notebook is open to a single question. It took me eleven months to choose, and it's short, and it frightens me, because it's the kind of question that breaks rule two, rule three, all the rules—the kind you only get to ask if you're willing to pay the entire price: *Mom, are you proud of me?*

No. I won't ask that either. It sets the weight on her shoulders, and she carried enough for two lifetimes. So instead: when the fourth ring comes, I'll answer, and she'll say *so tell me about your week,* and I will tell her about my week—the soup I made, the neighbor's terrible dog, the way the late sun comes through the west window at five o'clock and makes the whole room look briefly expensive. She'll do her little honking laugh. And when I hear the coins running low, the last quarter turning over in her fingers, I'll say the thing I've spent a year deciding on:

"I love you, Mom. Talk to you next year."

And I'll hang up first. For once, I'll be the one who has somewhere to be.

I should write something genuinely good—something with a voice, an arc or at least a shape, something that feels alive rather than generic. Since it's "whatever comes to me," I can lean into something evocative and strange.

Let me think about what would be interesting. Options:
1. A short story — perhaps something quiet and uncanny
2. A personal essay-style meditation
3. Something experimental in form
4. A piece of flash fiction about memory, time, loss

I think a short story with a distinctive voice would work best. Let me brainstorm premises:

- A lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the light itself
- A woman who inherits her grandmother's habit of naming storms
- A town where everyone's shadow arrives a few minutes late
- A translator who discovers a word in a dead language that means exactly the feeling of almost remembering
- A man who works at a lost-and-found for things people lost metaphorically (time, nerve, faith)
- The last day of a museum before closing, told from the perspective of the night guard
- Someone who writes letters to future occupants of their apartment
- A piano tuner who can hear when a house is sad
- A child who catalogs the sounds of a dying language spoken by one grandmother

I like the idea of something about memory and smallness—the lost-and-found for intangible things is charming but maybe too whimsical-clever. The piano tuner hearing houses is nice but maybe too precious.

Let me try: a story about a person whose job is to be the last speaker of something—or a witness. Or: "The Department of Almosts." Hmm.

Actually, let me try something quieter and stranger: a story about a man who repairs clocks and one clock that doesn't want to be fixed—a clock that runs slow on purpose, and he comes to understand why. That has emotional depth: grief, the desire for time to hold still.

Or: a woman who returns to her childhood home to pack it up after her mother's death, and finds that the house has been keeping things—every object triggers memory, and she realizes the house itself was a kind of memory machine. That's well-trodden though.

Title maybe: "Three Minutes of Change" or "Collect Call" or "The Payphone at Kettle Creek." A title is nice. "Coins" too plain. "Long Distance" — good, double meaning. Let's use "Long Distance."

Over the years I have learned the rules the way you learn anything that matters: by breaking them. Rule one, answer by the fourth ring, or nothing until next November—I tested that once, deliberately, the year I couldn't stand the wanting anymore, and paid for it with twelve months of silence. Rule two, never say how long it's been. The one time I slipped—"God, Mom, it's been twenty years"—she paused, confused, hurt, and then the static came up like water filling a sink, and I lost her early. Rule three: no questions about after. I asked once, softly, "Mom, are you okay, where are you—" and got the dial tone, flat and final as a dropped lid.

Rule four took longest: ask small questions. The big ones starve her. Did she find the blue scarf she lost in 1987? Yes—in her coat pocket, of course. Had Mr. Alvarez next door fixed his gutter? He had not; he'd put up a plastic owl instead. She told me the owl worked, which we both understood to be a lie, and I loved her so much in that moment I had to press my hand flat against the table to keep from making a sound.

I keep a notebook now. All year, questions accumulate and get ranked. In the early years the list was desperate: Are you happy. Do you know I'm sorry. What should I do about [name redacted, some wounds don't close]. Now the entries read more like weather: Ask about the owl. Ask if she remembers the beach house, the sand in the eggs. Ask her to hum it—the thing she hummed while cooking, tuneless, half a song. She'll say she doesn't remember humming anything, and then she'll hum.

Last year I noticed something I'd been avoiding. I'm fifty-four. She was fifty-three when the diner burned. Somewhere between one November and the next I aged past her, and now when she says You sound tired, honey, it comes from somewhere above me, a hand on the head of a grown man kneeling in his kitchen.

This is what I know about those calls, or believe, which may be the same thing: I don't think it's a message system. I used to hunt for meaning in every phrase—did she know, could she see me, was this purgatory or a porch. I gave up. What I've decided is simpler and harder: it's just her, with a handful of change, doing what she always did, which was check on me. Three minutes of checking on me. Everything else is my side of the wire.

November 9th falls on a Sunday this year. I've cleaned the apartment the way I would if she were visiting, which is ridiculous, and I've done it anyway. The notebook is open to a single question. It took me eleven months to choose it, and it isn't in my handwriting rhythm—it's short, and it frightens me, because it's the kind of question that might break rule two, rule three, all the rules, the kind of question you only get to ask if you're willing to pay the whole price:

"Mom, are you proud of me?"

No. I won't ask that either. It puts the weight on her, and God knows she carried enough. Here's what I'll do instead. When the fourth ring comes I'll answer, and she'll say "So tell me about your week," and I will tell her about my week—the soup I made, the neighbor's dog, the way the light comes through the west window at five and makes the whole room look briefly expensive—and she'll make her little honking laugh, and when I hear the coins running low, the last quarter turning in her fingers, I'll say what I've decided to say:

"I love you, Mom. Talk to you next year."

And I'll hang up first. For once, I'll be the one who has somewhere to be.
